senses.gloss:
loka
(‘world’)
------------------------------------------
See BHUVANA.
This word is also used in a more general sense, to indicate birth in a body capable of experiencing happiness and misery. It can also mean people in general.
Apart from the three worlds or the seven worlds or the fourteen worlds, the scriptures mention other types of worlds also. See CHĀNDOGYA UPANIṢAD (8.2).

lokasaṅgraha
(‘maintaining order in the society’)
------------------------------------------
This is a word peculiar to the Bhagavadgītā (3.20, 25).
Among the various counter-arguments that Śrī कृष्ण gives to अर्जुन to make him fight, लोकसङ्ग्रह is also one. It is interpreted as keeping the people within the orbit of धर्म and not allowing them to transgress it. This has to be achieved by the leaders of the society even if they have transcended it by attaining मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् by conforming themselves to the path of धर्म and thus induce or inspire the common people also to do the same.
In this context, if अर्जुन as a क्षत्त्रिय and a prince does not discharge his duty (to fight the evil-doers and destroy them), ordinary people in the society too, will do the same and abandon their duties and responsibilities. This will ultimately upset the whole social balance.

Lokāloka
(‘bright and dark’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् like Bhāgavatam (5.20) describe a mythical mountain called लोकालोक or चक्रवाल situated at the southernmost tip of the earth and bordering the sea. It is called चक्रवाल since it is circular in shape and is like hair to मोथेर् earth (cakra = circular; vāla = hair). Since one side of it is always bright (loka = bright) and the opposite side always dark (aloka = dark), it is also called ‘Lokāloka’. The sun always rises and sets within its circular barrier. The region beyond it is in perpetual darkness. This however is no obstacle to the spirits of the virtuous persons, who go to higher worlds.
